newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy faces chaotic two weeks of transport strikes.
newsitem.headline: Italy faces chaotic two weeks of transport strikes.

text.p: Air traffic controllers went on strike at 11 Italian airports on Monday at the start of what are set to be two chaotic weeks of stoppages by transport workers locked in contract disputes.

The eight-hour stoppage at Bari, Bologna, Cagliari, Catania, Genoa, Milan Malpensa, Naples, Bergamo, Palermo, Trieste and Turin had little effect on traffic since it was called by smaller controllers' unions.
But big delays were expected as a result of another planned eight-hour air traffic controllers' strike on Wednesday called by six main labour organisations.
Transport Minister Claudio Burlando was due to meet representatives of air traffic controllers' unions later on Monday to try and avert further strike action.
Burlando said he hoped dialogue would also prevail when he held a further meeting on Tuesday with railway workers who have called a 24-hour stoppage from the evening of April 19.
"I will ask them if it is possible to reopen talks to stop the strikes," he said.
"We are working to change what was a truce into a long-term agreement on a plan to change the Italian transport system, which is at the moment far behind other countries," he said.
Further national stoppages by bus, tram and metro drivers were planned for Thursday, followed next Monday by a four-day strike by petrol pump attendants.
Another strike by air traffic controllers was planned in Milan for Friday April 18 and a four-day sea transport strike was due to start on April 19.
Italian employers' group Confindustria condemned the industrial action and called on the government for intervention.
"Confindustria calls on the government and parliament for urgent intervention," it said in a statement.
"There has been continued unrest in this sector for years with no parallel in other industrialised countries."
It said the worsening action indicated the "absolute inadequacy of the existing method of dealing with union conflicts in the public sector".
